cmo-cmo-2016-01.prompt:
The integers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2016$ are written on a board. You can choose any two numbers on the board and replace them with their average. For example, you can replace $1$ and $2$ with $1.5$, or you can replace $1$ and $3$ with a second copy of $2$. After $2015$ replacements of this kind, the board will have only one number left on it.

(a) Prove that there is a sequence of replacements that will make the final number equal to $2$.

(b) Prove that there is a sequence of replacements that will make the final number equal to $1000$.
cmo-cmo-2016-01.answer: Any block $\{a, a+1, \ldots, b\}$ with $b \ge a + 2$ can be reduced to $a + 1$ (average $b-2, b$ into $b-1$, merge the two copies, then repeatedly average $k$ and $k+2$), and by symmetry to $b - 1$; for (b) reduce $\{1..999\}$ to $998$, $\{1001..2016\}$ to $1002$, then $998, 1000, 1002 \to 1000$.

cmo-cmo-2016-02.prompt:
Consider the following system of $10$ equations in $10$ real variables $v_1, \ldots, v_{10}$:
$$v_i = 1 + \frac{6v_i^2}{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \cdots + v_{10}^2} \qquad (i = 1, \ldots, 10).$$
Find all $10$-tuples $(v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_{10})$ that are solutions of this system.
cmo-cmo-2016-02.answer: $(\tfrac85, \ldots, \tfrac85)$ and the ten permutations of $(\tfrac43, \ldots, \tfrac43, 4)$ (nine entries $\tfrac43$).

cmo-cmo-2016-03.prompt: Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that $P(P(n) + n)$ is a prime number for infinitely many integers $n$.
cmo-cmo-2016-03.answer: $P(x) = p$ for a prime $p$, or $P(x) = -2x + b$ with $b$ odd. (Key fact: $P(n) \mid P(P(n) + n)$.)

cmo-cmo-2016-04.prompt:
**Lavaman versus the Flea.** Let $A$, $B$, and $F$ be positive integers, and assume $A < B < 2A$. A flea is at the number $0$ on the number line. The flea can move by jumping to the right by $A$ or by $B$. Before the flea starts jumping, Lavaman chooses finitely many intervals $\{m + 1, m + 2, \ldots, m + A\}$ consisting of $A$ consecutive positive integers, and places lava at all of the integers in the intervals. The intervals must be chosen so that:

(i) any two distinct intervals are disjoint and not adjacent;

(ii) there are at least $F$ positive integers with no lava between any two intervals; and

(iii) no lava is placed at any integer less than $F$.

Prove that the smallest $F$ for which the flea can jump over all the intervals and avoid all the lava, regardless of what Lavaman does, is $F = (n - 1)A + B$, where $n$ is the positive integer such that
$$\frac{A}{n + 1} \le B - A < \frac{A}{n}.$$
cmo-cmo-2016-04.answer: With $C = B - A$: each lava block must be cleared by one $B$-jump from $(L - C, L]$. If $F \le nA + C - 1$, Lavaman uses gaps of exactly $nA + C - 1$; the flea is then forced to make exactly $n$ jumps of $A$ between blocks, and its landing offset past each block grows by $1$, so it fails at block $C + 1$. If $F \ge nA + C$, every distance $d \ge nA$ can be covered to within $(d - C, d]$ by jumps $(u - v)A + vB$, so the flea clears every block.

cmo-cmo-2016-05.prompt: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with altitudes $AD$ and $BE$ meeting at $H$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$, and suppose that the circumcircles of $\triangle DEM$ and $\triangle ABH$ meet at points $P$ and $Q$ with $P$ on the same side of $CH$ as $A$. Prove that the lines $ED$, $PH$, and $MQ$ all pass through a single point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$.
cmo-cmo-2016-05.answer: For $X \in \{P, Q\}$: the line $XH$ meets $ED$ on the circumcircle $\Omega$ (directed-angle chase through the cyclic quadrilaterals $APDR$, $PBRE$), and the line $MX$ meets $\Omega$ on $ED$ (power of $M$: $MX \cdot MX^\wedge = MA \cdot MB = MD^2 = ME^2$). Since $ED$ meets $\Omega$ twice and $M, P, H$ are never collinear, $PH$ must pass through the point coming from $MQ$.
